title: Do Over

jokes.text: Hello, pussycat. / A lot of ladies get right in the car after that line, you creepy piece of... Jack!
jokes.setup: An unseen figure delivers a sleazy pickup line 'Hello, pussycat' at Liz from a car window
jokes.punchline: Liz is mid-insult when she realizes it's Jack, her boss — the creep is someone she knows and respects
jokes.explanation: Strong cold open. The misdirection works well — we assume a random creep, then the reveal recontextualizes Jack's character immediately. 'You creepy piece of...' cut off mid-sentence is economical and funny. Fits Jack's patrician obliviousness perfectly.

jokes.text: That information is classified at least until Cheney dies. Which is going to be a long time from now. That man is mostly metal.
jokes.setup: Liz asks how Jack got out of his government job; Jack says it's classified
jokes.punchline: The secret will be kept until Cheney dies — which won't be soon because 'that man is mostly metal'
jokes.explanation: Excellent topical joke with genuine wit. 'That man is mostly metal' is a perfect, absurd, quotable punchline — it gets the Cheney-as-robot joke to its logical extreme with maximum economy. Jack's delivery as a Republican insider who knows this firsthand makes it character-specific. One of the episode's strongest lines.

jokes.text: Devin is the worst. It's like he doesn't even care when we should have cake for people whose birthdays are on the weekend. / The Friday before. At lunch.
jokes.setup: Liz supports Jack coming back because Devin is a bad boss
jokes.punchline: Her evidence that Devin is the worst is his failure to properly schedule birthday cake — and she has a very specific rule about it
jokes.explanation: Perfectly Liz Lemon — her complaint about bad management is entirely about food logistics. The specificity of 'The Friday before. At lunch.' delivered as two staccato fragments escalates the comedy. Strong character integration; only Liz would define workplace dysfunction this way.

jokes.text: So what's with the outfit, Lemon? Did the people at that makeover show finally respond to your letter?
jokes.setup: Liz is dressed up for her home evaluation
jokes.punchline: Jack's explanation is that she wrote to a makeover show, implying her normal appearance is so bad she'd need to apply for professional help
jokes.explanation: Classic Jack-belittling-Liz beat. The 'your letter' detail implies she's been trying, unsuccessfully, for a while — which adds depth. Solidly constructed but not exceptional.

jokes.text: I got rid of all my Colin Firth movies in case they consider them erotica. That man can wear a sweater.
jokes.setup: Liz explains her home preparation for the adoption evaluation
jokes.punchline: She treats Colin Firth movies as potential erotica — justified by the understated, sincere coda 'That man can wear a sweater'
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. The premise (Colin Firth movies as erotica) is funny on its own, but 'That man can wear a sweater' as the sincere, minimalist justification is brilliant. It's both a perfect Liz character beat and a comedy writing masterclass in understatement. Highly quotable. The specificity of 'sweater' rather than anything overtly sexual is the genius move.

jokes.text: Only thing Kathy and I need assistance with is deciding which John Mayer song to do it to.
jokes.setup: Jack offers to assist Devin and Kathy
jokes.punchline: The only help they need is a sex playlist decision — and John Mayer specifically implies a certain douchey, clichéd taste
jokes.explanation: Efficiently characterizes Devin as a smug party-boy with bad taste. The John Mayer specificity does real work — it's a shorthand for a certain type of hollow alpha male. Clean construction.

jokes.text: You know what they say about rumors, Jack. They make a 'rue' out of 'more' and 'S.'
jokes.setup: Jack says rumor has it that Devin is in over his head; Devin deflects with a saying
jokes.punchline: Devin attempts the 'assume makes an ass of u and me' format but completely botches it with nonsense syllables that don't add up
jokes.explanation: Brilliant character joke. Devin is trying to use the classic 'assumptions' wordplay but produces complete gibberish ('rue,' 'more,' 'S' = 'rumors'?), which simultaneously makes no sense and reveals his fraudulence. The confidence with which he delivers it makes it funnier. Highly quotable absurdist non-logic.

jokes.text: Ah! Don't even think about talking to her when her soaps are on. Seriously, she will bite you.
jokes.setup: Jack and Devin are discussing Kathy Geiss (the CEO's daughter)
jokes.punchline: Kathy is so childlike/feral that she will literally bite people during her stories — treated as a casual warning
jokes.explanation: First introduction to the Kathy Geiss running gag. The casualness of 'she will bite you' is funny — it's matter-of-fact about something deeply weird. Sets up later payoffs well.

jokes.text: ...keep your friends close and your enemies so close that you're almost kissing.
jokes.setup: Devin starts to deliver the 'keep your friends close, enemies closer' maxim
jokes.punchline: He mangles it into something homoerotic and nonsensical — 'so close that you're almost kissing'
jokes.explanation: Second iteration of the Devin-botches-aphorisms gag. He takes a famous saying and makes it simultaneously homoerotic and meaningless. Consistent with the 'rumors' joke above — establishing Devin as someone who thinks he's being witty but is just generating nonsense.

jokes.text: So that's why I'm gonna offer you a job... in the mail room.
jokes.setup: Devin has been building to what seems like a power move or dismissal
jokes.punchline: The dramatic pause lands on the humiliation of 'the mail room' — a concrete demotion for a senior executive
jokes.explanation: Functional setup/punchline. The pause before 'in the mail room' does the structural work. Not particularly original but lands the beat.

jokes.text: I'll take it.
jokes.setup: Devin has just humiliated Jack by offering him a mailroom job
jokes.punchline: Jack's instant, unfazed acceptance — no hesitation, no wounded pride — reveals his total conviction in his own long game
jokes.explanation: Two words, perfectly placed. The maximum economy score is justified — there is not a single unnecessary syllable. Jack's complete lack of ego injury is both character-defining and funny. The joke is entirely in the confidence of the delivery.

jokes.text: I still don't know how that advertised Tokyo University.
jokes.setup: Tracy announces a residual check from a Japanese commercial he did
jokes.punchline: A cutaway presumably shows the absurd commercial; the button is Tracy's genuine bafflement at how it advertised a university
jokes.explanation: Classic 30 Rock cutaway structure. Tracy's bafflement at his own work is funny, and 'Tokyo University' is a specific enough absurd detail to elevate it. The visual gag (the commercial itself) is implied and likely very funny on screen.

jokes.text: But I'm gonna use this $300 to buy us all some boots for me.
jokes.setup: Tracy says he'll use his money to buy everyone something
jokes.punchline: Mid-sentence pivot — 'boots for me' — he forgot or never meant the 'us all' part
jokes.explanation: Compact Tracy character joke. The syntax breakdown mirrors his thought process — he almost does something generous and then just... doesn't. Tight and funny.

jokes.text: My video game is selling through the rizznoof! / Whoa, that's not slang. He has a speech impediment.
jokes.setup: Tracy uses 'rizznoof' as if it's street slang, like 'roof' in 'through the roof'
jokes.punchline: Frank corrects — it's not slang, Tracy has a speech impediment
jokes.explanation: Elegant misdirection. We assume Tracy is doing his usual made-up slang (a known character trait), but the reframe — speech impediment, not affectation — is a genuinely surprising and funnier explanation. Frank's deadpan correction sells it. Sets up the running gag beautifully.

jokes.text: I think I did it alone... and this check is the prizznoof. / Now that one was just him being obnoxious.
jokes.setup: Tracy uses 'prizznoof' again after the speech-impediment joke was established
jokes.punchline: Frank immediately distinguishes — this one was deliberate obnoxiousness, not impediment
jokes.explanation: The callback escalates the original joke. The meta-distinction between 'this is a real impediment' vs 'now he's just being obnoxious' is sophisticated comedy writing. Frank as the straight man who can decode Tracy is perfectly calibrated. The running gag payoff comes faster than expected, which makes it funnier.

jokes.text: The last time, it took me 22 years. But I know so much more now this time. I think I can do it in nine.
jokes.setup: Jack explains he can work his way back up from the mailroom
jokes.punchline: His optimistic timeline for clawing back to VP is nine years — presented as the fast-track
jokes.explanation: Good Jack joke. The specificity of 22 years vs nine makes the absurdity concrete. His total sincerity about a nine-year recovery plan being fast is funny. Character-specific — Jack's ambition is so pathological he treats this as reasonable.

jokes.text: And if my home evaluation goes well I will be a mother by 50. / We really can have it all.
jokes.setup: Jack says he'll be VP before 60; Liz mirrors with her own optimistic timeline
jokes.punchline: 'We really can have it all' — Jack's sincere feminist-adjacent affirmation about two wildly delayed, depressing timelines
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best structural jokes. Jack's 'we really can have it all' is a direct quote from empowerment culture, delivered with complete sincerity about two bleak situations. The irony is layered — it's funny, sad, and character-perfect all at once. Strong quotability.

jokes.text: How old are you, Liz? Thirty-seven. / I should tell you right now it's important that you don't lie.
jokes.setup: Bev asks Liz's age
jokes.punchline: Immediately after Liz answers truthfully, Bev warns her not to lie — implying 37 sounds like a lie (too old to be believable, or she assumed Liz was older/younger)
jokes.explanation: Precise timing joke. The beat — answer, then 'don't lie' — lands because we can't tell if Bev thinks she's lying or it's just her scripted spiel. The ambiguity makes it funnier and more uncomfortable.

jokes.text: How often do you entertain gentlemen sex guests? / Once a year maybe? But I'd be open to cutting that down.
jokes.setup: Bev asks a clinical question about Liz's sex life using the absurd euphemism 'gentlemen sex guests'
jokes.punchline: Liz's answer ('once a year') is so pathetically low — and her offer to reduce it for adoption purposes makes it worse
jokes.explanation: 'Gentlemen sex guests' is a brilliantly clinical euphemism. But the real laugh is 'once a year maybe' — the loneliness embedded in that answer is both funny and sad, and Liz's willingness to go even lower reveals her priorities.

jokes.text: You ever run a webcam ring outta here, Liz? Gentlemen tell you what to do, you do it? At first with some feigned hesitation?
jokes.setup: The adoption evaluation continues with increasingly invasive questions
jokes.punchline: The specificity of 'at first with some feigned hesitation' is the detail that makes this truly bizarre — this is a real form question, apparently
jokes.explanation: The escalating specificity of 'at first with some feigned hesitation' is the standout detail — it transforms a raunchy question into something almost procedurally weird. The phrase does a lot of work. Bev's clinical delivery of this absurdity is key.

jokes.text: I was arrested once in Germany for public nudity. I thought it was a topless beach. It was a shipyard.
jokes.setup: Asked if she's ever been convicted of a crime
jokes.punchline: 'It was a shipyard' — the location inversion makes the image absurdly specific and funny
jokes.explanation: Near-perfect joke construction. Three sentences, three beats. The setup is clean, the misdirection (beach vs. shipyard) is maximally absurd, and 'It was a shipyard' lands with perfect economy. Completely character-specific — only Liz would have this exact backstory. Highly quotable. One of the episode's top moments.

jokes.text: Is that a work call? / Could be. Or it could be my annual sex guest.
jokes.setup: Liz's phone rings during the evaluation
jokes.punchline: Liz jokes it might be her 'annual sex guest' — a callback to the once-a-year admission
jokes.explanation: Competent callback that keeps the running joke alive. 'Annual sex guest' is a good compression of the earlier joke. Not as funny as the original but earns its place.

jokes.text: Ms. Geiss, I have your Soap Opera Digest.
jokes.setup: Jack is making his pitch to Kathy Geiss about her father's wishes
jokes.punchline: Kenneth interrupts with Kathy's Soap Opera Digest — confirming the earlier warning about her soaps and her infantile tastes
jokes.explanation: Mild character joke that pays off the earlier soaps warning. Functional but not particularly strong on its own.

jokes.text: Liz wants everyone to be on their best behavior, leading to 'Nothing weird.' / Aw, come on, it's Movie Party Thursday. I brought in my tape of circus accidents.
jokes.setup: Liz asks the staff to be normal for Bev's visit
jokes.punchline: Frank's protest reveals Movie Party Thursday is a real recurring event, and his tape of circus accidents is the current feature
jokes.explanation: Sets up the running circus accidents gag. 'Movie Party Thursday' as an institutional event, with 'circus accidents' as the content, efficiently characterizes the writers' room as both communal and deeply weird.

jokes.text: No! Please. A lion eats a sad clown. Tomorrow.
jokes.setup: Liz says no to the circus accidents tape
jokes.punchline: Frank describes the climax of the tape — 'a lion eats a sad clown' — as if this is a compelling argument to keep watching
jokes.explanation: 'A lion eats a sad clown' is a genuinely funny image — the 'sad' qualifier is doing real work, making the clown pathetic before he even gets eaten. Frank's plaintive 'Tomorrow' is perfect economy. The specificity elevates it above generic dark humor.

jokes.text: Please, just be normal sauce for one day.
jokes.setup: Liz is pleading with her staff
jokes.punchline: 'Normal sauce' — not 'normal,' but 'normal sauce' — a random intensifier that is somehow exactly the kind of thing Liz would say
jokes.explanation: 'Normal sauce' is a delightfully weird coinage that feels specific to Liz Lemon's particular brand of desperation-speak. It's not trying to be slang or a reference — it's just an odd intensifier that lands because it's so unexpected. Highly quotable.

jokes.text: Oh, I told you not to write back to your stalker. / Oh, no, this is not about Yolanda.
jokes.setup: Jenna says she has a serious issue
jokes.punchline: Liz's assumption is that it's stalker-related — and the stalker has a name (Yolanda), implying ongoing correspondence
jokes.explanation: Quick character joke. The detail that the stalker has a name and that Liz knows not to write back suggests an established, accepted absurdity in Jenna's life. Economy of worldbuilding.

jokes.text: I mean, I don't do anything for Yolanda and she sends me those headless dolls.
jokes.setup: Jenna is complaining Tracy hasn't compensated her; she's using Yolanda as a comparison
jokes.punchline: The 'headless dolls' detail escalates the stalker joke from eccentric to genuinely threatening
jokes.explanation: Good escalation of the stalker bit. 'Headless dolls' is darkly specific and funny, especially because Jenna mentions it casually as a perk. The joke is that she's comparing Tracy's lack of generosity unfavorably to her stalker.

jokes.text: Can I hide this box of penis pasta in your dressing room?
jokes.setup: Scene transition — presumably following up on Liz's 'nothing weird' request
jokes.punchline: Frank's request makes no narrative sense except as a pure absurdist non-sequitur that shows the request has already failed
jokes.explanation: Pure absurdist line that lands on the specificity of 'penis pasta' as a product Frank owns and needs to relocate. The mundane request framing ('can I hide...') makes the content funnier. Maximum economy — it's six words and contains a complete joke.

jokes.text: She touched me. / Who? / Kathy Geiss, she touched me in my swimsuit area.
jokes.setup: Jack pulls Liz aside to whisper urgently
jokes.punchline: 'In my swimsuit area' — the childlike euphemism coming from Jack Donaghy is the entire joke
jokes.explanation: Exceptional joke. 'Swimsuit area' is the kind of clinical/childlike euphemism you'd find in a grade school health curriculum — coming from the supremely sophisticated Jack Donaghy, it's character comedy at its best. The contrast between Jack's persona and the language he uses is perfectly calibrated. Highly quotable. One of the episode's standout moments.

jokes.text: It's not at all erotic and fun, like when men do it to women.
jokes.setup: Jack is explaining why Kathy's advance was uncomfortable
jokes.punchline: His genuinely held belief that men groping women is 'erotic and fun' — stated without any self-awareness
jokes.explanation: Darkly satirical line. Jack's obliviousness is played perfectly straight — he genuinely believes this, which makes it both funnier and a pointed commentary on his character. The show gets away with this because Jack's worldview is clearly being satirized.

jokes.text: How far would I have to let her go to get my job back? Are we talking over the shirt? Frontsies, backsies? Or would I really have to give her my gift?
jokes.setup: Jack is seriously considering the calculus of how much he'd have to endure
jokes.punchline: The bases-style breakdown ('over the shirt,' 'frontsies, backsies') is absurdly juvenile for Jack, culminating in 'my gift' — a euphemism for something he considers precious
jokes.explanation: Excellent extended joke. The teenage-language taxonomy ('over the shirt,' 'frontsies, backsies') is wildly inappropriate for Jack, and 'my gift' as a final escalation is both absurd and somehow Jack-specific. The systematic approach to a disgusting calculation is perfectly character-integrated. One of the episode's top moments.

jokes.text: If I pleasure Kathy to get my old job, I'm no better than Devin.
jokes.setup: Jack talks himself into the virtuous path
jokes.punchline: The moral framework where 'pleasuring Kathy for advancement' is the ethical standard he's measuring against is both absurd and funny
jokes.explanation: Good character beat. The humor comes from Jack finding a meaningful ethical distinction within an already absurd situation. His sense of honor applied to something ridiculous is classic Jack.

jokes.text: Even if it takes five years. / I thought you said nine years? / I was promoted again this morning. I'm now Director of Mail Systems.
jokes.setup: Jack says the virtuous path will take five years
jokes.punchline: Liz catches the inconsistency with his earlier nine-year estimate; Jack explains a third promotion in one morning
jokes.explanation: Good callback to the escalating promotions gag. Jack's trajectory is so steep it's now compressing years — and Liz is tracking it closely enough to catch the discrepancy, which adds another layer.

jokes.text: Are these dolls? Are they? / Mommy. / They're called Little Creepers. Is it so wrong that I just want to have one of these to grow up and resent me? / Oh, you will.
jokes.setup: Liz encounters some unsettling dolls in the staged nursery
jokes.punchline: 'Is it so wrong that I just want to have one of these to grow up and resent me?' — Liz's extremely low bar for motherhood, confirmed by Pete's 'Oh, you will'
jokes.explanation: Excellent exchange. Liz articulating her aspiration as 'a child who resents me' is perfectly dark, perfectly Liz. Pete's 'Oh, you will' is a two-word confirmation that lands because it's so assured. The doll saying 'Mommy' adds a creepy-funny beat. Well-structured with a great button.

jokes.text: Hey, Tracy, did you see that thing in the paper today about how Lil' Wayne... that's a person, right?
jokes.setup: Liz is trying to use a pop culture reference to nudge Tracy into generosity
jokes.punchline: She pauses mid-sentence to confirm Lil' Wayne is a real person — revealing her total disconnect from pop culture she's trying to weaponize
jokes.explanation: Perfect character beat for Liz. She's trying to be culturally literate as a strategic move and can't even clear the basic hurdle. The question is guileless and the timing is perfect — right in the middle of the setup.

jokes.text: To the Batmobile! / Don't worry, he's just leasing it.
jokes.setup: Tracy dramatically announces their departure
jokes.punchline: Liz's 'Don't worry, he's just leasing it' implies Tracy actually has a Batmobile and this is a reasonable financial concern
jokes.explanation: Quick absurdist beat. Liz's response treats the Batmobile as real and addresses the one practical concern someone might have about it. Her matter-of-factness is the joke. Good economy.

jokes.text: Don't worry, he's just leasing it.
jokes.setup: Tracy announces 'To the Batmobile,' implying he actually has one
jokes.punchline: Liz's 'Don't worry, he's just leasing it' — her flat reassurance confirms there IS an actual Batmobile, but the concern she's addressing is financial responsibility, not the fundamental absurdity
jokes.explanation: The joke works on two levels: (1) Tracy Jordan actually has a Batmobile, and (2) Liz's response normalizes the absurdity by treating the lease status as the relevant detail. Her calm reassurance treats the car's existence as unremarkable while trying to seem responsible. Exceptional economy.

jokes.text: What I'm saying is don't dress for the job you have, dress for the job you want to have. So now, Manny... Tomorrow I show up for work dressed as a Mexican wrestler.
jokes.setup: Jack, in the mailroom, is dispensing wisdom to a coworker named Manny
jokes.punchline: Manny's takeaway from Jack's corporate wisdom is to show up as a Mexican wrestler — a complete logical leap that somehow follows
jokes.explanation: Jack dispensing executive wisdom to mailroom workers who misapply it is a good recurring concept. 'Mexican wrestler' as the specific aspiration is a funny left turn. The joke is partly Jack's confidence that he's mentoring effectively.

jokes.text: Banks, you've got to get a hold of yourself. / Oh, I'm running it. I have a plan to quadruple profits by the year 2015. / How are you possibly going to do that? / The old-fashioned way, Jack. I'm gonna shut it down. I'm gonna shut the whole thing down for two years.
jokes.setup: Jack finds Devin disheveled and shoeless, but Devin claims to have a business plan
jokes.punchline: The plan to 'quadruple profits' is to shut down the company entirely — presented with total confidence
jokes.explanation: Excellent Devin joke. 'The old-fashioned way, Jack' sets up an expectation of conventional business wisdom, then completely subverts it with the most counterintuitive plan possible. His confidence in the plan is the key ingredient.

jokes.text: I mean, imagine how badly people will want light bulbs then.
jokes.setup: Devin explains his plan to shut down GE for two years
jokes.punchline: His logic — create scarcity in light bulbs — has a twisted internal consistency that makes it funnier than pure nonsense
jokes.explanation: Good escalation of the previous joke. The light bulb scarcity logic is absurdly coherent — Devin has thought this through, which is scarier and funnier. GE's actual product being light bulbs adds a nice specificity.

jokes.text: It's just 'G' now, Jack. I sold the 'E' to Samsung. They're 'Samesung' now.
jokes.setup: Jack appeals to the gravity of GE as a company
jokes.punchline: Devin has already sold the letter 'E' to Samsung, which combined with their name makes 'Samesung'
jokes.explanation: The best joke in the episode. 'I sold the E to Samsung. They're Samesung now.' is a perfect piece of absurdist corporate comedy. The concept (selling a letter) is insane, but the execution — 'Samesung' as the actual result — follows its own logic impeccably. Supremely quotable, original, economical. This is the kind of joke 30 Rock was famous for.

jokes.text: I was supposed to be at a board meeting five hours ago. Which way's Connecticut?
jokes.setup: Devin is establishing how far gone he is
jokes.punchline: He doesn't know which direction Connecticut is — a casual geography question that confirms his total incompetence
jokes.explanation: Good button on the Devin scene. The geography question is a nice deflating detail — he's not just strategically incompetent, he's lost in every sense.

jokes.text: Three of my nine siblings were adopted. And someday, I'm gonna find them.
jokes.setup: Kenneth warmly endorses adoption to Bev
jokes.punchline: 'And someday, I'm gonna find them' — implying he's lost track of his adopted siblings, adding a dark twist to what was a sweet sentiment
jokes.explanation: Exceptional Kenneth joke. The setup is so earnest and sweet, the punchline so perfectly dark and understated. 'And someday, I'm gonna find them' lands perfectly because it's delivered with Kenneth's characteristic sincerity about something genuinely sad. The economy is near-perfect — the entire joke is one sentence.

jokes.text: Watch out, you idiot! Jackass! / We're like a big family here.
jokes.setup: Liz is giving Bev a warm tour of the studio, describing it as a family
jokes.punchline: Someone shouts 'Watch out, you idiot! Jackass!' right as Liz makes the 'big family' claim — immediately disproving it
jokes.explanation: Classic ironic juxtaposition gag. The timing of the outburst against the 'big family' claim is very well executed. Not highly original (it's a common sitcom beat) but the execution is crisp.

jokes.text: Hey, Rick. / I'm Fred. Rick is the other black guy. / Happens to everyone, right, Bev? / Yeah, happens all the time to my black husband.
jokes.setup: Liz misnames a Black crew member in front of Bev
jokes.punchline: Liz tries to normalize it as universal; Bev reveals her husband is Black and it doesn't 'happen all the time' to him — exposing Liz's racism
jokes.explanation: Sharp social comedy. Liz's defensive 'happens to everyone' is perfectly cringe, and Bev's correction (via her Black husband) is a precise, economical takedown. The joke makes a real point about Liz's well-intentioned but oblivious character. The setup and punchline are well-calibrated.

jokes.text: I first met Liz in 1993. She was fresh out of college and I had just broken up with O.J. Simpson. And can I just say something? Total gentleman.
jokes.setup: Jenna is giving a testimonial about Liz to Bev
jokes.punchline: She casually mentions she dated O.J. Simpson and that he was 'a total gentleman' — the darkest possible celebrity endorsement
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's very best jokes. Jenna treating her O.J. Simpson relationship as a casual biographical detail is already funny. 'Total gentleman' is the perfect punchline — it's wildly wrong given what O.J. is famous for, delivered with complete Jenna sincerity. The structure is impeccable: the 1993 timeline grounds it, the O.J. drop is the shock, and 'total gentleman' is the chef's kiss. Highly quotable and very dark.

jokes.text: Liz is a really, really mature person and she totally deserves to get custody of her kids. / It's not a custody case. Liz is trying to adopt a child. / Then who were those kids you were yelling at the other day? / Those were some child actors who had lied about being able to breakdance.
jokes.setup: Jenna's testimonial becomes increasingly problematic
jokes.punchline: The 'kids she was yelling at' were child actors who lied about breakdancing — a completely specific and absurd explanation that raises more questions
jokes.explanation: Excellent multi-beat joke. The 'custody' confusion is funny, but 'child actors who had lied about being able to breakdance' is the real punchline — a specific, vivid, completely plausible TGS scenario delivered as if it explains everything. The specificity ('lied about BEING ABLE TO breakdance') is the key ingredient.

jokes.text: Actually, I lived with Liz while I was separated from my wife. In a platonic way. But I haven't lived there for a couple months now because I've been at an anger management treatment center 'cause I shot one of my co-workers with an arrow.
jokes.setup: Pete is giving a testimonial meant to help Liz's adoption case
jokes.punchline: His helpful character witness testimony ends with 'I shot one of my co-workers with an arrow' — the most damaging possible button
jokes.explanation: Exceptional joke structure. Pete's testimonial escalates naturally from 'helpful detail' to 'slightly concerning' to 'completely disqualifying' in three sentences. The matter-of-fact 'cause I shot one of my co-workers with an arrow' as a subordinate clause in a character reference is masterful. The specificity of an arrow (not a gun) adds absurdist flavor. One of the episode's top jokes.

jokes.text: I think it's a circus in the Philippines. The lion goes nuts and attacks this older clown. How did we start talking about this? Did you bring it up?
jokes.setup: Frank is still discussing the circus accidents tape despite Liz's prohibition
jokes.punchline: The tape apparently involves a Philippines circus; Frank defensively asks who brought it up — strongly implying he did
jokes.explanation: Third beat of the circus accidents running gag. The Philippines specificity and 'older clown' detail add texture. 'Did you bring it up?' is the best moment — Frank can't stop talking about something he was told to stop talking about and tries to gaslight whoever he's speaking to.

jokes.text: I'm going upstairs to doink Kathy Geiss.
jokes.setup: Jack explains he has to take drastic action to save the company
jokes.punchline: 'Doink' — a deliberately childish/silly verb for what he's about to do, treating this corporate sacrifice with the same casual terminology as 'to the mail room'
jokes.explanation: The word 'doink' does all the work here. Jack's euphemism of choice is somehow both more and less dignified than expected. The matter-of-factness with which he announces this plan is classic Jack.

jokes.text: Frank, for all your hard work, please accept this set of solid gold nunchucks. / I will use these only for good.
jokes.setup: Tracy is giving out gifts to collaborators
jokes.punchline: Frank accepts solid gold nunchucks with complete sincerity, pledging to use them only for good
jokes.explanation: Two-part joke. 'Solid gold nunchucks' as a gift is perfectly Tracy. Frank's solemn oath — 'I will use these only for good' — is the perfect character response, implying the question of evil-use of nunchucks was even considered.

jokes.text: For letting us use the sound booth, please accept this chinchilla coat. / Wow. / You're gonna get so much nice-nice in that you're gonna have to grow another ding...
jokes.setup: Tracy gives Pete a chinchilla coat
jokes.punchline: Tracy's prediction for Pete's romantic success is cut off mid-sentence by Bev's arrival — but we know where it was going
jokes.explanation: The cutoff is the joke here. Tracy's mid-word interrupt ('ding...') both is and isn't a dirty joke — the audience completes it, which is funnier than hearing it. 'Nice-nice' as Tracy's euphemism is also good character work.

jokes.text: Now you look out for my girl, Liz Lemon. 'Cause me and her go way back, like spinal cords and car seats. / That's not really an expression.
jokes.setup: Tracy is earnestly vouching for Liz to Bev
jokes.punchline: 'Like spinal cords and car seats' — a simile that sounds meaningful but is completely random; Liz's correction ('that's not really an expression') is the button
jokes.explanation: Brilliant Tracy joke. 'Like spinal cords and car seats' has the rhythm and syntax of a genuine folk expression while being completely meaningless — Tracy is performing profundity with total conviction. Liz's flat correction ('that's not really an expression') is the perfect straight-man response. Highly quotable and original. One of the episode's standout moments.

jokes.text: Kenneth, it is imperative that you keep Mr. Banks down here. Do you know what imperative means? / Tell me, tell me! / Important. It means important.
jokes.setup: Liz gives Kenneth an urgent instruction
jokes.punchline: Kenneth doesn't know the word 'imperative' and asks with such eagerness that Liz has to give him a vocabulary lesson mid-crisis
jokes.explanation: Good Kenneth character beat. 'Tell me, tell me!' captures his enthusiastic helpfulness combined with stunning gaps in knowledge. The joke works because Kenneth is clearly going to try his hardest no matter what the word means.

jokes.text: Mr. Banks... look how many push-ups I can do.
jokes.setup: Kenneth has been tasked with keeping Devin occupied
jokes.punchline: His strategy is to demonstrate push-ups — a completely childlike distraction method that somehow works on Devin
jokes.explanation: Perfectly economical Kenneth joke. Nine words that establish: (1) Kenneth takes his task seriously, (2) his solution is absurdly childlike, (3) we're meant to infer Devin actually watches. The specificity of push-ups as Kenneth's chosen distraction is very funny. One of the episode's best Kenneth moments.

jokes.text: Devin's here! / Cover yourself.
jokes.setup: Jack is in Kathy's office, having apparently begun his 'doink' mission
jokes.punchline: 'Cover yourself' implies Jack has already been undressed or partially compromised — the visual implication is the joke
jokes.explanation: Good visual/implied joke. 'Cover yourself' as the immediate instruction upon Devin's arrival tells us everything about what Jack was up to without showing it. The implication is funnier than any explicit depiction.

jokes.text: You smell like strawberries. / That's the lip gloss she put on me so I could be her fancy boy.
jokes.setup: Liz encounters Jack after his mission
jokes.punchline: 'Her fancy boy' — Jack summarizes his humiliation in one phrase that is both Victorian-sounding and completely degrading
jokes.explanation: Great line. 'Her fancy boy' applied to Jack Donaghy is comedy gold — the aristocratic/Victorian phrasing is perfectly wrong for the situation. The strawberry lip gloss detail is a great sensory anchor. Jack's defeated delivery of this line is the final ingredient.

jokes.text: ...Dora the Explorer panties that were clearly made for an obese child.
jokes.setup: Jack describes what he witnessed/experienced with Kathy
jokes.punchline: Kathy's underwear is Dora the Explorer brand, sized for an obese child — the specificity is both funny and disturbing
jokes.explanation: Exceptional detail. 'Dora the Explorer panties that were clearly made for an obese child' is a very specific, very funny image that efficiently characterizes Kathy while also being viscerally funny. The 'obese child' qualifier is the key — it escalates it from 'adult wearing kids' underwear' to something even more specific.

jokes.text: No way, the best part of soap operas is when someone's twin interrupts a wedding. Or somebody pulls a gun at the fitness center.
jokes.setup: Jack suggests that soap operas are all about sex as a way to explain Kathy's motivation
jokes.punchline: Liz defends soap operas not for their sex but for twin-interrupted weddings and gym shootings — very specific soap opera tropes delivered as sincere preferences
jokes.explanation: Good Liz character joke. Her specific soap opera defenses — 'twin interrupts a wedding' and 'someone pulls a gun at the fitness center' — are both genuinely accurate soap opera tropes and exactly the aspects Liz would prioritize. The 'fitness center' location is the funny detail.

jokes.text: Kathy's texting me now. She's wondering where my strawberry mouth is.
jokes.setup: Jack and Liz are mid-conversation
jokes.punchline: 'Strawberry mouth' — Kathy's pet name for Jack, tied to the lip gloss, is both absurd and degrading
jokes.explanation: Good callback. 'Strawberry mouth' as Kathy's nickname for Jack crystallizes his new role. The callback to the lip gloss detail makes the nickname land harder.

jokes.text: This is what you're giving me as a thank you gift? Some coupons for free hugs? / I'm suing you for my share of your video game profits, Tracy.
jokes.setup: Tracy has given Jenna something as a thank-you; Liz had said something special was planned
jokes.punchline: The special gift was free hug coupons — so bad it immediately pivots Jenna to lawsuits
jokes.explanation: Good payoff to the setup about Tracy's special gift. 'Coupons for free hugs' as the big reveal is perfectly cheap. Jenna going from outrage to lawsuit in one beat is good character writing.

jokes.text: Would you like to see the green room? / What? / You mean the nursery! / We gotta get this stuff back to the rental place by 5:00.
jokes.setup: Liz is trying to manage Bev's tour while multiple problems converge
jokes.punchline: Pete simultaneously reveals the nursery is a rental AND there's a deadline, compounding the crisis
jokes.explanation: Competent escalation beat. Pete's rental deadline revelation is a good joke but somewhat functional — it moves the plot while getting a laugh.

jokes.text: Ms. Lemon, did you lie to me about there being a nursery here? / No! / Rick, what are you doing? / Bitch, my name is Fred.
jokes.setup: The nursery ruse is collapsing; Liz tries to save it
jokes.punchline: Liz makes the same mistake again — calling Fred 'Rick' in front of Bev at the worst possible moment
jokes.explanation: Excellent callback with escalation. Liz repeating the exact same mistake in front of the same evaluator, in the middle of a crisis, is perfect. 'Bitch, my name is Fred' is the most emphatic possible callback button. The raised stakes make it funnier than the original.

jokes.text: Kathy, Bev and I are just friends. / Kathy's the new CEO of our company. / Bev, you better run. She's surprisingly strong.
jokes.setup: Kathy Geiss appears and seems to misinterpret Bev's presence as romantic competition
jokes.punchline: 'She's surprisingly strong' — Jack's warning implies Kathy is physically dangerous and he knows this from experience
jokes.explanation: Good Kathy Geiss character beat. 'She's surprisingly strong' is funny because it implies Jack has already learned this the hard way, and treating Kathy like a dangerous animal that Bev should flee from is a good comic image.

jokes.text: Frank, I told you to change that hat!
jokes.setup: Chaos has broken out; Liz is still trying to manage the situation
jokes.punchline: Amid the crisis, Liz's priority is still Frank's hat — a callback to the earlier instruction and a good indication of her misplaced focus
jokes.explanation: Running gag callback that works on economy alone. One line in the middle of chaos that tells us Liz is still tracking everything. Not a big laugh but a solid running gag beat.

jokes.text: God, how can I have a kid here? I can't even keep a grown woman safe in this place.
jokes.setup: The evaluation has descended into chaos with Bev getting hurt
jokes.punchline: Liz's existential realization that her failure to protect an adult adoption evaluator from workplace violence undermines her case for being trusted with a child
jokes.explanation: Liz's self-aware moment of clarity that's both funny and genuinely pathetic. The logic is impeccable — if you can't keep a middle-aged woman safe from a feral CEO, you probably can't handle a child. Works as both joke and character beat.

jokes.text: Oh... / I'm Bev. I'm here to do Liz's adoption evaluation. / Ah! All right, take her to the hospital. / Let's get started!
jokes.setup: Bev has apparently suffered a fall and hit her head; she resets completely
jokes.punchline: Bev re-introduces herself with total amnesia; Liz's brief, hopeful 'no we have to take her to the hospital' vs. Bev's peppy 'Let's get started!' creates the setup for the do-over
jokes.explanation: Good structural joke. The head injury reset is an absurdist plot mechanism and the episode commits to it. 'Let's get started!' after reintroducing herself is a funny, chipper button.

jokes.text: Do-over! Do-over, she doesn't remember anything! You heard what the lady said, we're taking a mulligan. Let's make this one count now.
jokes.setup: Bev's amnesia presents an unexpected opportunity
jokes.punchline: Liz's excited invocation of 'do-over' and 'mulligan' — childlike playground language applied to a deeply unethical situation — is the joke
jokes.explanation: Good Liz character moment. The episode is titled 'Do Over' and this is the explicit invocation — the meta-connection adds a small bonus. Her giddy rule-bending, justified in the most childlike terms, is very in-character.

jokes.text: I'm gonna give Kathy the full soap opera while you try to trick a lady with a head injury.
jokes.setup: Jack and Liz are dividing their tasks
jokes.punchline: 'Try to trick a lady with a head injury' — Jack's plain summary of Liz's plan is funny because it strips away all her rationalizations
jokes.explanation: Excellent line. Jack, who is about to sexually manipulate a mentally child-like CEO, summarizes Liz's plan in the most damning possible terms. The juxtaposition — Jack's even worse plan vs. his judgment of Liz's — is the comedy.

jokes.text: We might not be the best people. But we're not the worst? / Graduate students are the worst.
jokes.setup: Liz and Jack acknowledge the ethically compromised plans they're both about to execute
jokes.punchline: Jack's response — the worst are graduate students — is a specific, confident, and completely non-sequitur answer to Liz's question
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's very best jokes, close to the top. Jack's confident assertion that graduate students are the worst — offered as genuine comfort to Liz's moral anxiety — is perfectly Jack. The class snobbery, the specificity (not criminals, not murderers — graduate students), and the utter confidence of it make it exceptional. Jack Donaghy could only say this and mean it. Highly quotable. Near-perfect economy.

jokes.text: She reminds me of my own mom. Tough love, consistency, a little moustache in a certain light.
jokes.setup: Kenneth gives a character testimonial about Liz for the do-over evaluation
jokes.punchline: The comparison to his mom includes 'a little moustache in a certain light' — a specific physical detail that is both an insult to Liz and a strange detail about Kenneth's mother
jokes.explanation: Very good Kenneth joke. 'A little moustache in a certain light' is an excellent specific detail — it's meant as a compliment (comparing her to mom) but inadvertently insults both Liz and describes his mother. The 'in a certain light' qualifier makes it funnier than a flat statement would be.

jokes.text: And her other kids really like her. / What?
jokes.setup: Kenneth is wrapping up his glowing testimonial
jokes.punchline: 'Her other kids' — implying Liz already has children, which she categorically does not
jokes.explanation: Quick Kenneth joke. His casual mention of Liz's 'other kids' lands because it's so definitively wrong and said with such confidence. Bev's flat 'What?' is the right response. Good economy.

jokes.text: Oh... I'm Bev. I'm here to do Liz's adoption evaluation. / Ah! All right, take her to the hospital.
jokes.setup: Bev has reset again — a second time — after the do-over already produced its result
jokes.punchline: Bev resets yet again; this time Liz immediately gives up and takes her to the hospital
jokes.explanation: Good triple-beat running gag. The joke is Liz's immediate pivot — she got what she needed from the do-over, and when Bev resets a third time, she doesn't even try to exploit it. It efficiently closes the Bev storyline.

jokes.text: Kathy is my partner. She's hiring me to advise her in all her business matters. / I'm sorry, darling. I've been paranoid ever since that incident with the weather machine. / Kiss, kiss, kiss!
jokes.setup: Jack is trying to wrap up the soap opera performance and secure his deal
jokes.punchline: Kathy is still in soap opera mode — 'that incident with the weather machine' is a perfect soap opera trope delivered by Kathy as if real; 'Kiss, kiss, kiss!' is her directing them like a soap opera scene
jokes.explanation: Great Kathy Geiss moment. 'The incident with the weather machine' is a perfect soap opera non-sequitur. 'Kiss, kiss, kiss!' as Kathy's direction is both funny and reveals how completely she lives in this fictional world. The scene perfectly uses the soap opera theme established throughout.

jokes.text: No... No, thank you.
jokes.setup: Kathy demands Jack and Liz kiss
jokes.punchline: Jack's polite but firm 'No, thank you' — the most civilized possible refusal, as if declining dessert — is the joke
jokes.explanation: Perfect Jack economy. 'No, thank you' as his response to being commanded to kiss Liz is exactly the right level of dignified refusal. The pause before 'No' adds timing. Pure character comedy.

jokes.text: Got any mail for me, Donaghy? / It's all over, Banks.
jokes.setup: Devin arrives to gloat about Jack being in the mailroom
jokes.punchline: Jack's 'It's all over, Banks' — delivered from a position of apparent defeat — is both a reversal and a classic Jack power move
jokes.explanation: Good reversal beat. Devin's sneering mailroom question is immediately neutralized by Jack's authority. The contrast between Jack's setting (mailroom) and his confidence is the joke.

jokes.text: I'm gonna sue you! I'm going to sue the entire city of New York! I'm gonna sue you! / You can't sue me, I'm already being sued. / Double indemnity!
jokes.setup: Devin discovers he's been outmaneuvered; Tracy apparently has something to do with it
jokes.punchline: Tracy's 'You can't sue me, I'm already being sued' as a legal defense; Devin's 'Double indemnity!' as a made-up counter-argument
jokes.explanation: Excellent absurdist legal exchange. Tracy's logic ('already being sued' as immunity) is perfectly Tracy, but Devin's 'Double indemnity!' as a desperate counter-move — using a film title as if it's a legal term — is the gem. Both characters are simultaneously ridiculous and completely in character.

jokes.text: Unfortunately, Bev has made a full recovery. So I have to start over with another agency.
jokes.setup: Jack asks how Liz's friend Bev is
jokes.punchline: 'Unfortunately' — Liz's use of 'unfortunately' about a person's full recovery reveals how much she was banking on the amnesia
jokes.explanation: Exceptional joke. One word — 'unfortunately' — does all the work. It's a completely revealing character moment: Liz was hoping this woman with a head injury wouldn't recover, and she says so plainly, accidentally, as an opener. The economy (9.5) is justified — the punchline is a single word. One of the episode's standout moments.

jokes.text: The semi-virtuous path.
jokes.setup: Jack and Liz reflect on their outcomes; Liz says she'll start over
jokes.punchline: 'The semi-virtuous path' — Jack's coinage characterizes their moral standard as something definitionally less than virtuous but better than nothing
jokes.explanation: Great callback and coinage. 'Semi-virtuous path' as their shared standard is a perfect philosophical summary of the episode. Jack's ability to rationalize anything in elevated language is on full display. Highly quotable.

jokes.text: Did you need something else, Lemon? / No, I just like seeing you in there.
jokes.setup: Liz lingers after their conversation; Jack notices
jokes.punchline: Liz simply enjoys seeing Jack back in his office — a sincere, slightly sentimental statement that's funnier for being stated so plainly
jokes.explanation: Good closing beat. Liz's plainly stated affection for Jack is both funny and warm. 'I just like seeing you in there' lands as a dry but genuine statement of their partnership. Perfect economy for a closing line.

jokes.text: Did you need something else, Lemon? / No, I just like seeing you in there.
jokes.setup: Jack is settled back in his office; Liz lingers in the doorway
jokes.punchline: Liz's 'I just like seeing you in there' — a genuine, unguarded moment of warmth that's funnier because she delivers it without sentimentality, as a simple fact
jokes.explanation: Perfect episode-closing joke. The comedy is in Liz's emotional honesty delivered without performance — she just says it flatly, which makes it simultaneously funny and warm. Character integration is excellent: this is exactly how Liz would express genuine affection, and only Liz and Jack's relationship earns this beat. One of the softer jokes of the episode but one of the most satisfying.

tmdb_overview: Worried that Liz's hectic lifestyle may be too much to adopt a child, Bev, the adoption agent, visits the set. Panicked, Liz tells everyone to act normal, but chaos soon ensues as a fight arises between Jenna and Tracy. Meanwhile, Jack returns to 30 Rock and vows to do whatever it takes to get his position back from Devin.
insight: Season 3 premiere launches with 61 jokes in 23 minutes—2.63-per-minute pace sustains 90+ humor.
